title: Probing Physics Beyond the Standard Model through Combined Analyses of Next-Generation Type Ia Supernova, CMB, and BAO Surveys
comment: 23 pages, 13 figures; Comments welcome; The likelihood code, associated data products, and plotting scripts can be downloaded from https://github.com/sriniraghunathan/CMB_BAO_SNe_likelihoods
summary: Observations of Type Ia supernovae (SNIa), baryon acoustic oscillations (BAO), and the cosmic microwave background (CMB), which probe the late-, intermediate-, and early-universe epochs, respectively, provide complementary constraints on the expansion history of the Universe. In this work, we forecast constraints on dark energy and other extensions to the standard cosmological model by combining the SNIa sample expected from the Vera C. Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST), data from current and forthcoming CMB surveys, and BAO measurements from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI). For the CMB, we use temperature, polarization, and lensing power spectra ($TT/EE/TE/φφ$) from South Pole Telescope, the planned Advanced Simons Observatory, and a CMB-S4-like experiment. We derive constraints on $Λ{\rm CDM}$ and its extensions involving the dark energy equation of state parameters $(w_{0}, w_{a})$ and the sum of neutrino masses $\sum m_ν$, using a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling framework. We find that the LSST Year-3 SNIa sample can improve upon the DES Year-5 dark energy constraints by a factor of $\times2-\times2.5$, with the gains driven primarily by the significantly higher SNIa density in the LSST sample. Similarly, DESI-DR3 shows up to a $\times1.8$ improvement on dark energy parameters over DR2, driven largely by the substantial increase in low-redshift sample. Combining CMB with LSST-Y3-SNIa and DESI-DR3-BAO yields $σ(w_{0}) = 0.028$ and $σ(w_{a}) = 0.11$ for $w_{0} w_{a} {\rm CDM}$ cosmology with the results being largely independent of the CMB dataset. The constraints weaken by 10%-30% when freeing $\sum m_ν$ and spatial curvature. Moreover, the joint analysis of the three datasets can enable a $2-3σ$ detection of $\sum m_ν$.

AI.tldr: LSST SNIa, DESI BAO, and CMB data forecasts show significant improvements in dark energy constraints, with LSST-Y3 SNIa providing 2-2.5× better constraints than DES-Y5, and joint analysis enabling 2-3σ neutrino mass detection.
AI.motivation: To forecast constraints on dark energy and extensions to ΛCDM cosmology by combining complementary probes from different cosmic epochs: LSST SNIa (late universe), DESI BAO (intermediate universe), and CMB surveys (early universe).
AI.method: Used Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling framework to derive constraints on ΛCDM and its extensions (w₀, wₐ dark energy parameters and Σmν neutrino masses) by combining forecasted data from LSST Year-3 SNIa sample, DESI-DR3 BAO measurements, and CMB power spectra (TT/EE/TE/φφ) from SPT, Advanced Simons Observatory, and CMB-S4-like experiments.
AI.result: LSST-Y3 SNIa improves DES-Y5 dark energy constraints by factor 2-2.5; DESI-DR3 shows up to 1.8× improvement over DR2. Combined CMB+LSST-Y3-SNIa+DESI-DR3-BAO yields σ(w₀)=0.028 and σ(wₐ)=0.11 for w₀wₐCDM. Constraints weaken by 10-30% when freeing Σmν and spatial curvature. Joint analysis enables 2-3σ detection of Σmν.
AI.conclusion: The combination of LSST SNIa, DESI BAO, and CMB data provides powerful complementary constraints on dark energy and cosmological parameters, with LSST's high SNIa density driving significant improvements and enabling neutrino mass detection at 2-3σ significance.

title: Epicyclic Density Variations in the Indus Stellar Stream
comment: 18 pages, 16 figures, 3 supplementary movies, accepted by MNRAS
summary: Longitudinal density fluctuations observed in stellar streams can result from gravitational interactions with massive perturbers in the Milky Way, such as dark matter subhalos. Analysing these density variations provides a powerful probe of properties (motion, mass, size, etc.) of the perturbing objects. However, caution is needed because density variations may arise naturally from internal dynamics of streams, namely epicycles. In this work, we focus on the Indus stellar stream, a remnant of an ancient dwarf satellite of the Galaxy. An Indus stream spanning $\sim 90^\circ$ is revealed in the southern Galactic sky using a comprehensive matched-filter analysis utilizing data from the Gaia mission. A spatial density model is fitted to the filtered map to quantitatively characterize the morphology, which demonstrates episodic density peaks and gaps in the stream. Through N-body simulations, we show that there are strong epicyclic motions of stars happening during tidal disruptions. The present-day longitudinal densities from simulations are comparable to the measurement from data, with similar numbers and locations of peaks and gaps, suggesting that the observed density should mainly be caused by epicycles. We also find that a cuspy dark matter halo for the Indus dwarf is likely to produce milder stellar epicyclic peaks compared to a cored halo which results in steeper peaks. This arises from different instantaneous mass loss due to distinct central mass distributions of halos, where a cored halo usually leads to severer tidal stripping. The observed density exhibits moderate peak sharpness, implying that Indus may have originally possessed a cuspy halo.

AI.tldr: The Indus stellar stream's observed density fluctuations are likely caused by epicyclic motions from tidal disruption rather than dark matter subhalo interactions, with peak sharpness suggesting the progenitor dwarf galaxy had a cuspy dark matter halo.
AI.motivation: To determine whether density fluctuations in stellar streams like Indus result from gravitational interactions with dark matter subhalos or from internal epicyclic dynamics during tidal disruption, and to use these density variations to probe the dark matter halo profile of the progenitor dwarf galaxy.
AI.method: Used Gaia mission data with comprehensive matched-filter analysis to reveal the Indus stream spanning ~90°, fitted spatial density models to characterize morphology, conducted N-body simulations to model tidal disruption and epicyclic motions, and compared simulated density patterns with observations.
AI.result: Observed episodic density peaks and gaps in the Indus stream are comparable to N-body simulation results, suggesting density variations are mainly caused by epicyclic motions rather than dark matter subhalo interactions. The moderate peak sharpness implies the progenitor dwarf galaxy likely had a cuspy dark matter halo rather than a cored one.
AI.conclusion: Density fluctuations in the Indus stream primarily arise from epicyclic motions during tidal disruption, not from dark matter subhalo interactions. The observed peak sharpness suggests the Indus dwarf progenitor had a cuspy dark matter halo, providing insights into dwarf galaxy formation and dark matter properties.

title: POLAR-II: modeling star formation history of galaxies on the 21-cm signal from Epoch of Reionization
comment: 10pages, 8 figures; A&A accepted
summary: Galaxies may suffer some starburst and quenched periods in their history due to e.g. galaxy mergers and feedback. However, semi-numerical simulations of the Epoch of Reionization (EoR) typically do not accurately model the effects of the star formation history (SFH) of galaxies. Keeping the same total ionizing photon budget from galaxies, we investigate how the ionization and heating of the Intergalactic Medium (IGM), as well as the associated 21-cm signal during the EoR, depends on the variations in the modeling of the SFH of galaxies. We adopt the Jiutian-300 N-body dark matter simulation and the semi-analytic model L-Galaxies 2020 to model galaxy formation. Using the galaxy catalog from L-Galaxies 2020 as input, we post-process the Jiutian-300 density field with the one-dimensional radiative transfer code Grizzly to model the reionization process and the 21-cm signal. We find that the ionized regions produced by galaxies with a SFH derived from L-Galaxies 2020 are slightly larger and warmer than the ones obtained with a constant SFR. For a fixed stellar mass, galaxies produce smaller ionized regions with increasing stellar mass weighted stellar age $τ_{\rm age}$. This results in a different topology and timing of the IGM ionization and heating obtained from Grizzly. The SFH of galaxies is highly dependent on $τ_{\rm age}$ and redshift. Different models of the galactic SFH affect the gas heating and ionizing processes during the EoR, and as a consequence also the 21-cm global signal and power spectrum.

AI.tldr: Different star formation history models affect EoR ionization/heating and 21-cm signals despite same total ionizing photon budget.
AI.motivation: Semi-numerical EoR simulations typically don't accurately model galaxy star formation history effects on IGM ionization and heating.
AI.method: Use Jiutian-300 N-body dark matter simulation with L-Galaxies 2020 semi-analytic model for galaxy formation, post-process density field with Grizzly 1D radiative transfer code to model reionization and 21-cm signals.
AI.result: L-Galaxies SFH produces slightly larger, warmer ionized regions than constant SFR; for fixed stellar mass, older galaxies produce smaller ionized regions; SFH affects IGM ionization/heating topology and timing, impacting 21-cm global signal and power spectrum.
AI.conclusion: Galaxy SFH modeling significantly influences EoR ionization/heating processes and 21-cm observables, highlighting importance of accurate SFH representation in reionization simulations.

title: Testing Screened Modified Gravity with Strongly Lensed Gravitational Waves
summary: Screening mechanisms are essential components in many modified gravity theories, which satisfy local tests of General Relativity (GR) and address cosmic acceleration on cosmological scales. The strong gravitational lensing of gravitational waves (GWs) offers a unique observational probe into cosmology and fundamental physics. In this paper, we investigate the possibility of testing screened modified gravity theories with strongly lensed gravitational waves. Specially, we develop the refined theoretical and statistical framework, in order to measure the post-Newtonian parameter $γ_{\text{PN}}$ in the presence of screening effects. Specially, the mass-truncated power-law and Navarro-Frenk-White (NFW) models are introduced to quantify the modified lensing potential. Our analysis also addresses the mass-sheet degeneracy (MSD) problem, by incorporating the absolute magnification and time delay measurements accessible through strongly lensed GW systems. We find that individual lensed GW system detected by next-generation GW detectors can provide stringent constraints on the PPN parameter ($γ_{\text{PN}}$) across different screening scales ($Λ$). Therefore, future measurements of strongly lensed GWs have great promise to seek departures from GR on kpc-Mpc scales, due to more precise time delay from lensed GW signals.

AI.tldr: Testing screened modified gravity theories using strongly lensed gravitational waves to measure post-Newtonian parameter γPN and constrain screening scales.
AI.motivation: Screening mechanisms allow modified gravity theories to satisfy local GR tests while explaining cosmic acceleration, but need observational probes. Strong gravitational lensing of GWs offers unique opportunities to test these theories on kpc-Mpc scales.
AI.method: Develop refined theoretical and statistical framework to measure γPN with screening effects. Use mass-truncated power-law and NFW models for modified lensing potential. Address mass-sheet degeneracy using absolute magnification and time delay measurements from strongly lensed GW systems.
AI.result: Individual lensed GW systems detected by next-generation GW detectors can provide stringent constraints on γPN across different screening scales (Λ). Future measurements promise to detect departures from GR on kpc-Mpc scales due to precise time delays from lensed GW signals.
AI.conclusion: Strongly lensed gravitational waves are a powerful probe for testing screened modified gravity theories, with next-generation detectors offering precise constraints on post-Newtonian parameters and screening mechanisms.

title: Forward-modelling Milky Way Cepheids: selection effects and physical priors in the Gaia-HST calibration
comment: 20 pages, 6 figures, 5 appendices. To be submitted to MNRAS
summary: The advent of high-precision Gaia parallaxes for Milky Way Cepheids enables per cent-level calibration of the local distance ladder and $H_0$. We revisit the Milky Way Cepheid calibration from Gaia EDR3 parallaxes using a fully forward-modelled Bayesian framework that simultaneously infers the period--luminosity relation, the Gaia parallax zero-point offset, and individual stellar distances while explicitly incorporating the disk geometry of the Galaxy through the distance prior and the selection functions specified in two distinct HST SH0ES campaigns. We derive an analytic treatment of the detection probability that accounts for magnitude, parallax, period, and extinction cuts and reduces the selection treatment to a tractable integral over distance and sky position. Posterior predictive checks show that this generative model matches well the observed distributions of parallaxes, magnitudes, and periods. Modelling Galactic structure and survey truncation self-consistently in a Bayesian framework yields period--luminosity parameters that agree with the SH0ES maximum-likelihood values at the ${<}0.5\,σ$ level, a consequence, we show, of the small intrinsic scatter of the Cepheid period--luminosity relation. Adopting, as recently advocated, a uniform-in-volume prior without simultaneously accounting for selection leads to a ${\sim}\,0.05~\mathrm{mag}$ bias in the period--luminosity zero-point and posterior predictive distributions incompatible with the observed data; this shift is mostly driven by the omission of the selection model. A consistent Bayesian treatment of Galactic structure and selection effects reinforces the local distance-ladder determination of $H_0$, and hence the Hubble tension with early-Universe inferences.

AI.tldr: Bayesian forward modeling of Milky Way Cepheids with Gaia EDR3 parallaxes yields consistent period-luminosity relation with SH0ES, reinforcing Hubble tension when accounting for Galactic structure and selection effects.
AI.motivation: High-precision Gaia parallaxes enable percent-level calibration of the local distance ladder and H₀, but require careful treatment of Galactic structure and selection effects to avoid biases in Cepheid period-luminosity relation calibration.
AI.method: Fully forward-modelled Bayesian framework simultaneously infers period-luminosity relation, Gaia parallax zero-point offset, and individual stellar distances, incorporating Galactic disk geometry through distance prior and HST SH0ES selection functions with analytic treatment of detection probability.
AI.result: Period-luminosity parameters agree with SH0ES maximum-likelihood values at <0.5σ level; uniform-in-volume prior without selection accounting causes ~0.05 mag bias; consistent Bayesian treatment yields posterior predictive distributions matching observed data.
AI.conclusion: Proper Bayesian modeling of Galactic structure and selection effects reinforces local distance-ladder H₀ determination, strengthening Hubble tension with early-Universe inferences.

title: Stellar age determination using deep neural networks: Isochrone ages for 1.3 million stars, based on BaSTI, MIST, PARSEC, Dartmouth and SYCLIST evolutionary grids
comment: 17 pages, 13 figures
summary:
We aim to develop a model-driven deep learning approach to age determination, by training neural networks on stellar evolutionary grids. Contrary to the usual data-driven deep learning approach of using prior age estimates as training data, our method has the potential for a wider and less biased range of application. The low computational cost of deep learning methods compared to bayesian isochrone-fitting allows for a broad analysis of large spectroscopic catalogues.
  We train multilayer perceptrons on different stellar evolutionary grids to map [M/H], MG, (GBP - GRP) to stellar age $τ$. We combine Gaia photometry and parallaxes, metallicities and $α$ elements from spectroscopic surveys and extinction maps, which are passed through the neural networks to estimate stellar ages.
  We apply our method to the LAMOST DR10, GALAH DR3 & DR4 and APOGEE DR17 spectroscopic surveys, for which we estimate the ages using the BaSTI tracks, along with other stellar evolutionary models. We leverage this novel technique to study, for the first time, differences in age estimates from several evolutionary grids applied on very large datasets. In addition, we date 13 open clusters and one globular cluster and find a median absolute deviation with literature ages of 0.20 Gyr. Along with the stellar ages catalogues from our estimates, we release NEST (Neural Estimator of Stellar Times), a python package to estimate stellar age based on this work, as well as a web interface.
  We show that, when using the same evolutionary grid, our method retrieves the same ages as a bayesian approach like SPInS, for only a fraction of the computational cost, with a 60,000 speedup factor for a typical star. This model-driven deep learning technique thus opens up the way for broad galactic archeology studies on the largest datasets available today and in the near future with upcoming surveys such as 4MOST.

AI.tldr: A model-driven deep learning approach for stellar age determination using neural networks trained on evolutionary grids, achieving 60,000× speedup over Bayesian methods while maintaining accuracy.
AI.motivation: To develop a more efficient and less biased method for stellar age determination compared to traditional Bayesian isochrone-fitting, enabling broad analysis of large spectroscopic catalogues for galactic archaeology studies.
AI.method: Train multilayer perceptrons on stellar evolutionary grids (BaSTI tracks and others) to map [M/H], MG, (GBP - GRP) to stellar age τ. Combine Gaia photometry/parallaxes, spectroscopic metallicities, α elements, and extinction maps as inputs to neural networks for age estimation.
AI.result: Applied to LAMOST DR10, GALAH DR3/DR4, and APOGEE DR17 surveys; achieved median absolute deviation of 0.20 Gyr with literature ages for 13 open clusters and one globular cluster; demonstrated 60,000× speedup factor over Bayesian approach (SPInS) while retrieving same ages when using same evolutionary grid.
AI.conclusion: The model-driven deep learning technique (NEST package) enables efficient, accurate stellar age estimation for large datasets, opening new possibilities for galactic archaeology studies with current and upcoming surveys like 4MOST.

title: The statistics and structure of dissipation in subsonic and supersonic turbulence
comment: 14 pages, 8 figures, Article accepted for publication in MNRAS
summary: Turbulence plays a critical role in the atmosphere, oceans, engineering, and astrophysics. The dissipation (heating) induced by turbulent flows is particularly important for the thermodynamics and chemistry of interstellar clouds, yet its structure and statistics remain poorly understood. Using high-resolution turbulence simulations with controlled explicit viscosity, we study the kinetic energy dissipation rate, $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{kin}}$, across subsonic and supersonic regimes. We find that dissipation lags large-scale kinetic energy injection events by $1.64\pm0.21$ and $0.48\pm0.07$ turbulent turnover times in subsonic and supersonic turbulence, respectively. Correlations show $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{kin}}\propto\vert\nabla\times\mathbf{v}\vert^2$ (vorticity squared) in the subsonic regime, where density fluctuations are negligible, while in the supersonic regime dissipation is primarily correlated with density, $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{kin}}\proptoρ^{3/2}$. A spectral analysis demonstrates that achieving numerical convergence of $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{kin}}$ across all scales is challenging, especially in the subsonic case, even at $2048^3$ resolution. Nonetheless, subsonic dissipation is clearly localised on small vorticity-dominated scales, while supersonic dissipation spans many scales, combining elongated, thin shocks with small-scale vorticity. Finally, we determine the fractal dimension of $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{kin}}$. In the subsonic regime, intense dissipation is predominantly organised in flattened vortex filaments embedded in thin shearing layers on small scales, becoming more volume-filling at larger scales. In the supersonic regime, $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{kin}}$ exhibits a fractal dimension between 1 and 2 across nearly all scales, likely reflecting shock surfaces and their intersections forming filaments.

AI.tldr: High-resolution turbulence simulations reveal fundamental differences in kinetic energy dissipation between subsonic and supersonic regimes, showing different time lags, scaling relations with vorticity vs density, and distinct spatial structures.
AI.motivation: Turbulent dissipation is crucial for interstellar cloud thermodynamics and chemistry, but its structure and statistics remain poorly understood despite its importance across atmospheric, oceanic, engineering, and astrophysical contexts.
AI.method: High-resolution turbulence simulations with controlled explicit viscosity were conducted to study kinetic energy dissipation rate (ε_kin) across subsonic and supersonic regimes, using spectral analysis and fractal dimension calculations up to 2048³ resolution.
AI.result: Dissipation lags large-scale energy injection by 1.64±0.21 turnover times (subsonic) vs 0.48±0.07 (supersonic). Subsonic dissipation scales with vorticity squared (ε_kin ∝ |∇×v|²), while supersonic scales with density (ε_kin ∝ ρ³/²). Subsonic dissipation localizes on small vorticity scales; supersonic spans many scales combining shocks and vorticity. Fractal dimensions differ: subsonic shows flattened vortex filaments, supersonic shows fractal dimension 1-2 reflecting shock surfaces.
AI.conclusion: Turbulent dissipation exhibits fundamentally different physics in subsonic vs supersonic regimes, with distinct time delays, scaling relations, spatial structures, and fractal properties, highlighting the need for regime-specific modeling approaches for astrophysical applications.

title: Obscured Star Formation in the Dwarf Galaxy DDO 43? A Comparative UV-IR Analysis
comment: 8 pages, 4 figures, published in Astronomische Nachrichten
summary: We present a study of recent star formation in the dwarf irregular galaxy DDO 43 using GALEX FUV and WISE NIR imaging. We identify regions of elevated FUV flux, indicating unobscured star-forming activity across much of the galaxy. To further characterize the stellar content, we compare the FUV fluxes to archival WISE W1 and W2 infrared data across 56 regions of interest. A general correlation is found between the FUV and infrared fluxes, suggesting spatially coherent star formation throughout the galaxy. A few regions, however, show elevated infrared fluxes but little or no UV emission, potentially indicating localized, dust-obscured star formation.

AI.tldr: Study of recent star formation in dwarf irregular galaxy DDO 43 using GALEX FUV and WISE NIR imaging reveals both unobscured and potentially dust-obscured star-forming regions.
AI.motivation: To investigate recent star formation activity in the dwarf irregular galaxy DDO 43 by combining ultraviolet and infrared observations to identify both unobscured and potentially dust-obscured star-forming regions.
AI.method: Used GALEX FUV imaging to identify regions of elevated FUV flux indicating unobscured star formation, then compared FUV fluxes to archival WISE W1 and W2 infrared data across 56 regions of interest to characterize stellar content and identify potential dust-obscured star formation.
AI.result: Found elevated FUV flux across much of DDO 43 indicating widespread unobscured star formation. General correlation between FUV and infrared fluxes suggests spatially coherent star formation. Some regions show elevated infrared fluxes but little/no UV emission, potentially indicating localized dust-obscured star formation.
AI.conclusion: DDO 43 exhibits both unobscured star formation visible in FUV and potentially dust-obscured star formation detectable only in infrared, with generally coherent spatial distribution of star-forming activity throughout the galaxy.

title: Going Wide and Deep with Roman: The z~6-9 UV luminosity function in a Roman Deep Field
comment: 31 pages, 12 figures, including 3 figure sets that are included in the appendix for the arxiv version. Submitted to ApJ
summary: We present a trade study of possible ultra-deep surveys with the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, optimizing the depth-area-filter parameter space for high-redshift galaxy science. Using a mock galaxy catalog derived from a 2 sq. degree lightcone created using the Santa Cruz semi-analytic model and populated with over 7.6 million galaxies at 0<z<10 with M_UV < -15, with realistic clustering and synthetic photometry, we evaluate sixteen 500-hour survey configurations spanning 0.28-2 sq. degrees and four filter combinations. We demonstrate that even a single Roman pointing dramatically reduces cosmic variance compared to HST-like observations, more faithfully recovering the true UV luminosity function. For each survey configuration, we explore photometric redshift recovery, sample contamination, and measurements of the rest-UV luminosity function and non-ionizing UV luminosity density across four redshift bins at z~6-9. We find that inclusion of the R062 filter is essential for studies at z~5-6, reducing sample contamination from nearly 100% to negligible levels and recovering the bright end of the luminosity function. The F184 filter improves galaxy recovery at z>9 and is critical for stellar contamination removal at all redshifts. Based on these results, we recommend that a Roman ultra-deep survey cover at least two Roman pointings (0.56 sq. degrees) with all six filters (R062, Z087, Y106, J129, H158, F184), reducing uncertainties on the rest-UV luminosity density by factors of 2-4 relative to the deepest existing JWST programs. Building off of the Deep Tier of the High Latitude Time Domain Survey to add depth and filter coverage to existing (or planned) observations is an excellent option.

AI.tldr: Roman Space Telescope ultra-deep survey optimization study shows that covering at least 0.56 sq. degrees with all six filters dramatically reduces cosmic variance and improves high-redshift galaxy science, with specific filters critical for different redshift ranges.
AI.motivation: To optimize ultra-deep survey configurations for the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope to improve high-redshift galaxy science by reducing cosmic variance and improving measurements of UV luminosity functions and densities.
AI.method: Used a mock galaxy catalog from a 2 sq. degree lightcone created with the Santa Cruz semi-analytic model, containing over 7.6 million galaxies at 0<z<10. Evaluated sixteen 500-hour survey configurations spanning 0.28-2 sq. degrees and four filter combinations, analyzing photometric redshift recovery, sample contamination, and UV luminosity measurements.
AI.result: Single Roman pointing dramatically reduces cosmic variance compared to HST. R062 filter is essential for z~5-6 studies, reducing contamination from nearly 100% to negligible levels. F184 filter improves galaxy recovery at z>9 and is critical for stellar contamination removal. Recommended survey: at least 0.56 sq. degrees with all six filters, reducing uncertainties on UV luminosity density by factors of 2-4 relative to deepest JWST programs.
AI.conclusion: An ultra-deep Roman survey covering at least two pointings (0.56 sq. degrees) with all six filters is recommended, with building off the Deep Tier of the High Latitude Time Domain Survey being an excellent option to enhance existing observations.

title: Mass regulates the emerging timescale of young star clusters
comment: 4 main figures; 2 extended data figures; 1 extended data table; accepted for publication
summary: Quantifying the timescales of star cluster emergence from their natal clouds remains one of the main challenges in our understanding of the star formation process. These timescales are fundamental measurements of the star formation cycle within galaxies, yet they are difficult to constrain due to the complex interplay between stellar feedback and star formation across a vast range of physical scales. Here we present HST and JWST observations of thousands of young star clusters in four nearby galaxies (M51, M83, NGC 628, and NGC 4449). A substantial fraction of these clusters are still embedded within their natal gas and remain invisible at optical wavelengths. We constrain their emergence process by measuring the timescales required to disperse the surrounding material. We find a strong correlation between dispersal timescale and cluster stellar mass, with massive clusters emerging more rapidly than their lower mass counterparts. This is a critical constraint on simulations of star formation and stellar feedback, which struggle to fully reproduce the formation and emergence of star clusters. Our results emphasize the central role of massive clusters in driving the escape of ionizing radiation into the galactic medium. Finally, they impose important limitations to the time available for planet formation in massive cluster environments where disks get exposed to UV irradiation and further gas infall is shut off.

AI.tldr: Study uses HST/JWST observations to measure timescales for star clusters to emerge from natal gas clouds, finding massive clusters emerge faster than low-mass ones, with implications for feedback simulations and planet formation.
AI.motivation: Quantifying timescales of star cluster emergence from natal clouds is a fundamental challenge in understanding star formation, as these timescales measure the star formation cycle but are difficult to constrain due to complex feedback processes across multiple scales.
AI.method: Used Hubble Space Telescope (HST) and James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) observations of thousands of young star clusters in four nearby galaxies (M51, M83, NGC 628, and NGC 4449). Measured emergence timescales by tracking how long clusters take to disperse surrounding natal gas material.
AI.result: Found strong correlation between dispersal timescale and cluster stellar mass: massive clusters emerge more rapidly than lower mass counterparts. Many clusters remain embedded in natal gas and invisible at optical wavelengths. Results provide critical constraints for simulations of star formation and feedback.
AI.conclusion: Massive clusters play central role in driving ionizing radiation escape into galactic medium. Findings impose important limitations on time available for planet formation in massive cluster environments, where protoplanetary disks get exposed to UV irradiation and further gas infall is shut off.

title: A Modified Conveyor Belt Model: Implications for Surface Density Thresholds for Massive Star Formation
comment: 17 pages, 17 figures, accepted for publication in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society
summary: Recent models and simulations of cluster formation within molecular clumps consider multi-scale, hierarchical accretion, which leads to clump mass growth over time. This mode of mass accumulation could have implications regarding the evolution of observable properties such as mass and radius, bringing into question the interpretation of commonly cited thresholds for high-mass star formation. In this paper, we use the conveyor belt model of cluster formation to create synthetic cores/clumps and derive physical and observational properties. We show that while this model successfully predicts many observed trends, modifications are required to match properties of high-mass prestellar clumps. When the model clumps are observationally classified as intermediate- or high-mass star-forming, the threshold delineating these two groups agrees with those found in the literature; however, results show that high-mass clumps at early evolutionary stages can be misclassified using standard surface density thresholds. Our logistic regression analysis reveals the quantity of material to ever enter a star-forming region is the most important factor in differentiating intermediate- and high-mass star-forming regions. This implies observations characterising the environment surrounding star-forming regions are crucial, especially at early evolutionary stages.

AI.tldr: The conveyor belt model of cluster formation shows that hierarchical accretion affects observable properties, potentially causing misclassification of high-mass prestellar clumps using standard surface density thresholds, with surrounding material being the key differentiator between intermediate- and high-mass star-forming regions.
AI.motivation: To investigate how hierarchical accretion in molecular clumps affects the interpretation of observable properties and thresholds for high-mass star formation, particularly addressing potential misclassification issues in early evolutionary stages.
AI.method: Used the conveyor belt model of cluster formation to create synthetic cores/clumps and derive their physical and observational properties, followed by logistic regression analysis to identify key differentiating factors.
AI.result: The model successfully predicts many observed trends but requires modifications for high-mass prestellar clumps. While thresholds for intermediate- vs. high-mass star-forming regions agree with literature, early-stage high-mass clumps can be misclassified using standard surface density thresholds. Logistic regression shows the total material ever entering a region is the most important factor for differentiation.
AI.conclusion: Observations characterizing the environment surrounding star-forming regions are crucial, especially at early evolutionary stages, as the quantity of material that will ever enter a region is the key factor distinguishing intermediate- from high-mass star-forming regions.

title: The role of mass loss in constraining quenching time in dwarf galaxies from AGB and RGB star counts
comment: Accepted for publication on Astronomy & Astrophysics. 16 pages, 12 figures
summary:
The capability of reconstructing the past star formation history of dwarf elliptical galaxies
  out of the Local Volume relies on modelling bright stellar populations currently
  evolving through the red giant branch (RGB) and the asymptotic giant branch (AGB) phases.
  Recent studies proposed the use of the relative fractions of RGB and AGB stars populating
  specific boxes in the observational colour-magnitude plane to infer the epoch within
  which 90\% of the stellar population of the galaxy formed (T90).
  We aim at understanding the physical process of stellar evolution that are constrained by
  the relationship between the relative fraction of AGB and RGB stars of dwarf galaxies and
  the T90 epoch.
  We use updated stellar models that include the description of dust formation in the
  wind, to undertake a population synthesis approach, to allow monitoring the variation of the
  NAGB/NRGB ratio with time. The effects of some specific ingredients, such as
  the mass loss experienced by low-mass stars during the RGB phase, and the details of the
  time variation of the star formation rate, are extensively explored and tested against
  data.
  The mass lost by low-mass stars during the RGB evolution proves the most
  relevant ingredients affecting the time variation of NAGB/NRGB: at
  metallicities ~ 1/10 solar, a mass loss ~ 0.25Msun is required to reproduce the observations. This
  analysis allows to derive a relationship between NAGB/NRGB and T90, with a ~ 1 Gyr uncertainty on T90.

AI.tldr: The study analyzes how the ratio of asymptotic giant branch (AGB) to red giant branch (RGB) stars in dwarf elliptical galaxies relates to their star formation history, finding that mass loss during RGB evolution is crucial for matching observations and enabling T90 epoch determination with ~1 Gyr uncertainty.
AI.motivation: To understand the physical stellar evolution processes underlying the relationship between AGB/RGB star ratios in dwarf elliptical galaxies and the epoch when 90% of their stellar population formed (T90), which is used to reconstruct past star formation histories.
AI.method: Population synthesis approach using updated stellar models that include dust formation in stellar winds, monitoring NAGB/NRGB ratio variation with time. Extensive exploration of specific ingredients: mass loss during RGB phase and details of star formation rate time variation, tested against observational data.
AI.result: Mass loss by low-mass stars during RGB evolution is the most relevant factor affecting NAGB/NRGB time variation. At metallicities ~1/10 solar, mass loss ~0.25 solar masses is required to reproduce observations. The analysis yields a relationship between NAGB/NRGB and T90 with ~1 Gyr uncertainty on T90 determination.
AI.conclusion: The study establishes a physical basis for using AGB/RGB star ratios to determine star formation histories in dwarf elliptical galaxies, identifying RGB mass loss as the key parameter and providing a calibrated relationship with quantifiable uncertainty.

title: Resolved molecular gas and star-formation in massive unquenched spirals : I. UGC 8179
comment: Accepted in A&A, 21 pages, 14 figures
summary: Recent studies have uncovered a rare population of super-massive (M* > 1e11 Msun) star-forming spiral galaxies, Super Spiral Galaxies (SSGs), whose existence challenges classical quenching scenarios. We investigate the resolved star-forming and molecular-gas properties of UGC 8179 (z=0.052, log(M*/Msun)=11.62) and assess whether its local star formation (SF) follows the same physical processes as typical Star-Forming Main Sequence (SFMS) spirals. We combined the first NOEMA CO(1-0) interferometric observations of an SSG with pixel-by-pixel SED fitting, based on archival UV-to-mid-IR imaging. Our 3"x3" pixel maps provide resolved measurements of M*, SFR and molecular gas surface densities across its extended disc. UGC 8179 hosts a massive rotating molecular gas reservoir of M_H2 = 1.02 1e10 Msun, yielding a standard molecular gas fraction, with typical depletion time \sim 1 Gyr in the observed region, despite its extreme mass. We derived lower limits of log(fmol) > -1.61 \pm 0.06 and log(tdep) > -8.82 \pm 0.13 at the scale of the galaxy. The large spatial extent of UGC 8179 enables us to probe low surface-density regimes hardly accessible in nearby disks (Σ* < 1e7 Msun / kpc2 ; Σ_SFR < 1e-3.5 Msun/yr/kpc2). All three resolved scaling relations (rSFMS, rKS and rMGMS) are well defined. The rKS slope (0.87 \pm 0.09) is broadly consistent with unity, indicating standard local SF processes. The rSFMS shows a shallower global slope (0.80 \pm 0.02) due to a central suppression in sSFR (~ -0.5 dex). This break suggests the influence of a bulge, driving a transition to a more dynamically regulated SF regime in the inner disc. UGC 8179 provides evidence that SSGs can sustain standard local SF processes while exhibiting central dynamical regulation at high stellar surface densities.

AI.tldr: Super-massive spiral galaxy UGC 8179 shows standard local star formation processes despite its extreme mass, with central star formation suppression suggesting bulge-driven dynamical regulation.
AI.motivation: Investigate whether super-massive star-forming spiral galaxies (SSGs) follow the same physical star formation processes as typical Star-Forming Main Sequence spirals, challenging classical quenching scenarios.
AI.method: Combined NOEMA CO(1-0) interferometric observations with pixel-by-pixel SED fitting using archival UV-to-mid-IR imaging to create resolved maps of stellar mass, star formation rate, and molecular gas surface densities across the extended disc.
AI.result: UGC 8179 hosts massive rotating molecular gas reservoir (M_H2 = 1.02×10^10 Msun) with typical depletion time ~1 Gyr. Resolved scaling relations show standard local star formation processes (rKS slope ~0.87), but shallower global rSFMS slope (0.80) due to central sSFR suppression (~ -0.5 dex).
AI.conclusion: SSGs can sustain standard local star formation processes while exhibiting central dynamical regulation at high stellar surface densities, likely driven by bulge influence, providing evidence against classical quenching scenarios for these extreme systems.

title: Far-infrared Polarization Properties of Nearby Star-forming Regions: A New Compendium of SOFIA/HAWC+ Observations
comment: 23 pages, 14 figure
summary: We present a comprehensive polarimetric study of 26 nearby molecular clouds in four far-infrared bands (53 $μ$m to 214 $μ$m) using 52 archival SOFIA/HAWC+ datasets. Far-infrared dust polarization observations probe the plane-of-sky magnetic field. To investigate scale-dependent trends, we group the molecular clouds by distance and analyze the data at common angular ($25''$) and common physical (0.052 pc and 0.32 pc) resolutions. The two shorter wavelengths are more impacted by smoothing, exhibiting a larger decrease in percent polarization. We analyze the polarization spectrum -- the polarization fraction as a function of wavelength -- and find that it depends more strongly on column density than dust temperature. We find a "falling" spectrum at the 0.052 pc resolution, but find a "flat" spectrum at the 0.32 pc resolution, suggesting that resolution plays an important role in the observed polarization spectra. We propose that warm dust grain emission in small-scale structures ($\lesssim$ 0.1 pc) traces different magnetic field geometries only resolved in our close regime data. There is no preferred magnetic field orientation across our data, which suggests that the magnetic field in our $\sim$ parsec scale regions is decoupled from the large-scale field that is primarily parallel to the Galactic plane. The relationship between percent polarization and column density varies between clouds, but the correlation between percent polarization and angular dispersion is consistent across regions. This compendium of dust polarization maps highlights the value of observing at multiple far-infrared wavelengths and will enable additional population-level studies of magnetic fields and dust across star-forming environments.

AI.tldr: Far-infrared polarimetric study of 26 nearby molecular clouds using SOFIA/HAWC+ data reveals that polarization spectra depend on column density more than dust temperature, and resolution significantly affects observed spectral shapes, with small-scale structures showing different magnetic field geometries.
AI.motivation: To investigate magnetic field properties in molecular clouds through far-infrared dust polarization observations, examining scale-dependent trends and the relationship between polarization spectra and physical parameters like column density and dust temperature.
AI.method: Analysis of 52 archival SOFIA/HAWC+ datasets covering 26 nearby molecular clouds in four far-infrared bands (53-214 μm). Data analyzed at both common angular (25") and common physical resolutions (0.052 pc and 0.32 pc) to study scale-dependent effects. Polarization spectra analyzed as a function of wavelength, with correlations examined between polarization fraction, column density, dust temperature, and angular dispersion.
AI.result: Shorter wavelengths more impacted by smoothing with larger polarization decrease. Polarization spectrum depends more strongly on column density than dust temperature. "Falling" spectrum at 0.052 pc resolution but "flat" spectrum at 0.32 pc resolution, indicating resolution's important role. No preferred magnetic field orientation across data, suggesting magnetic field at parsec scales is decoupled from large-scale Galactic field. Relationship between percent polarization and column density varies between clouds, but correlation between percent polarization and angular dispersion is consistent across regions.
AI.conclusion: Warm dust grain emission in small-scale structures (≲0.1 pc) traces different magnetic field geometries only resolved in close regime data. This compendium highlights the value of multi-wavelength far-infrared polarization observations and enables population-level studies of magnetic fields and dust in star-forming environments.

title: Black Hole Properties of Type-1 Active Galactic Nuclei in the North Ecliptic Pole Wide Field: I. Mid-infrared Sources with Optical Counterparts
comment: 20 pages, 10 figures, Accepted for publication in ApJS
summary: We present measurements of black hole (BH) properties of 861 Type-1 active galactic nuclei (AGNs) in the North Ecliptic Pole (NEP)-Wide field. These AGNs are detected in both optical and mid-infrared (MIR) surveys and are identified as Type-1 AGNs in optical spectroscopic surveys. By performing spectral energy distribution (SED) and line fitting, we obtained their MIR continuum luminosities ($L_{\rm MIR}$) as well as full width at half maximum (FWHM) values for the \ion{C}{4}, \ion{Mg}{2}, H$β$, and H$α$ lines. Using these measurements, we derived bolometric luminosities ($10^{43.20}$--$10^{47.27}~{\rm erg~s^{-1}}$), BH masses ($10^{7.29}$--$10^{9.67}$\,$M_{\odot}$), and Eddington ratios ($10^{-2.74}$--$10^{-0.08}$) for $\sim$450 objects over a wide redshift range ($z=0.09$--$4.71$). The use of $L_{\rm MIR}$ and FWHM values effectively alleviates the effects of dust extinction, enabling reliable estimates of BH properties even for dust-obscured AGNs. Moreover, we find that 34\,\% of the Type-1 AGNs in the NEP-Wide field are dust-obscured, and that their bolometric luminosities can be significantly underestimated without proper dust extinction correction. Our relatively extinction-free BH property estimates can (i) be combined with multi-wavelength data in the NEP-Wide field to facilitate diverse studies of AGN environments, number densities, host galaxies, and related topics, and (ii) serve as fiducial estimates for SPHEREx and other upcoming infrared (IR) spectroscopic missions covering the NEP-Wide field.

AI.tldr: Study of 861 Type-1 AGNs in NEP-Wide field using MIR continuum luminosities and emission line widths to derive dust-extinction-free black hole properties, revealing 34% are dust-obscured.
AI.motivation: To obtain reliable black hole property estimates for AGNs by overcoming dust extinction issues that typically bias optical measurements, particularly for dust-obscured objects.
AI.method: Used spectral energy distribution (SED) fitting and line fitting to measure MIR continuum luminosities (L_MIR) and FWHM values for CIV, MgII, Hβ, and Hα emission lines from optical and mid-infrared surveys of 861 Type-1 AGNs.
AI.result: Derived bolometric luminosities (10^43.20-10^47.27 erg s^-1), BH masses (10^7.29-10^9.67 M⊙), and Eddington ratios (10^-2.74-10^-0.08) for ~450 objects across z=0.09-4.71; found 34% of Type-1 AGNs are dust-obscured with significantly underestimated luminosities without proper extinction correction.
AI.conclusion: MIR-based measurements effectively mitigate dust extinction effects, providing reliable BH property estimates for dust-obscured AGNs; these extinction-free estimates will support multi-wavelength studies and serve as fiducial references for future IR spectroscopic missions like SPHEREx.
